name: Anaa-ti
notes: Location given as 22° 15′ S, 137° 30′ W, in the Tuamotus. Believed to be a mistaken sighting of a nearby island.

name: Antillia
coord_source: hand-approx: mid-Atlantic as on the 1424 Pizzigano chart
notes: The island, like the more popular Atlantis, is a fictional island in the Atlantic originating from an Iberian legend.

name: Antonio d'Ulloa Island
removed_evidence: 78° 20′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1875.
notes: Discovered by the Spanish captain Antonio de Ulloa at 37° 02′ S, 78° 20′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1875.

name: Arthur Island
notes: Location given by Arrowsmith as 3° 30′ S, 176° W. Noted to be needing confirmation of existence and position in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Atlantis
coord_source: hand-approx: just beyond the Pillars of Hercules (Plato); see Atlantis dataset
notes: Ancient Greek legend described by Plato, later hypothesized to be real, and depicted on a 1664 map by Athanasius Kircher.

name: Aurora Islands
notes: Discovered by Spanish merchant ship Aurora, currently thought to be the Shag Rocks.

name: Bacalao
notes: Gaspar Frutuoso noted its discovery by João Vaz Corte-Real in 1472 in Saudades da Terra.

name: Bale of Cotton
removed_evidence: cally gone onto it. Doubtful by 1817 and not s
coord_source: from notes: 5°22′N and 100 leagues east of Galle
notes: A rock in the mouth of the Bay of Bengal, located at 5° 22′ N "100 leagues east from Pointe de Galle." A passenger on the boat that saw the rock claimed to have physically gone onto it. Doubtful by 1817 and not seen on modern maps.

name: Bermeja
notes: Discovered in the early 16th century by Spain, but mysteriously vanished sometime during the 17th century. While no dominant theory holds, it is possible that the island submerged due to tectonic movements, supported by the existence of a seamount at and the nearby Scorpion Reef.

name: Bonetta Rocks
removed_evidence: rde and Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.
notes: Location given as 16° 32′ N, 20° 57′ W, between Cape Verde and Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.

name: Bradley Land
notes: A mass of land named by Frederick Cook which he claimed to have seen between () and () during a 1909 expedition.

name: Brasil or Hy-Brasil
notes: Said to lie in the Atlantic Ocean west of Ireland. Irish myths described it as cloaked in mist except for one day every seven years, when it became visible but still could not be reached. Several 16th century maps showing the island of Brasil also showed an island labelled Demar further south-west.

name: Britomart Island
removed_evidence: 50' W. Noted to be doubtful in 1851; not seen
notes: Discoverer unknown; location given as 19° 52' S, 145° 50' W. Noted to be doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Buss Island
notes: Found in the waters near Greenland, in which Martin Frobisher, the leader of the island-finding expedition, probably made a mistake in dead reckoning and mistook optical effects near Greenland for a new island.

name: Island of California
coord_source: hand-approx: Baja California (real land drawn as an island)
notes: A misconception about the Baja California Peninsula being an island due to an assumption that the Gulf of California was instead a strait separating California from the rest of the Americas.

name: Cassiterides
notes: Ancient source of Phoenician tin. Exact location unknown but thought to have possibly referred to now silt-connected islands within the marshes of Brière.

name: Clark's Reef
notes: Discoverer unknown, location given as 8° 18′ S, 139° 50′ (or 52′) W. Admiral Du Petit Thouars could not find the reef, sounding 200 fathoms.

name: Cloate's Island
notes: Various locations; sometimes 21° 30′ S, 92° 42′ E, in the Indian Ocean, west of Australia. Probably the headland now known as Point Cloates.

name: Crockerland
notes: A hoax invented by Arctic explorer Robert E. Peary to gain more financial aid from George Crocker, one of his financial backers.

name: Davis Land
notes: Supposedly sighted by the pirate Edward Davis in the Pacific along the southern latitude of 27 to 28 degrees, which was on the same latitude as the Spanish-controlled gold mines of Copiago. At the time, it was believed that gold could be found elsewhere along the latitude so several navigators were instructed to seek it out on their voyages. Never found, it was also believed by William Dampier to be the coast of Terra Australis Incognita.

name: Isle of Demons
notes: Probably a relocated version of the island of Satanazes (see island below).

name: Denia/Davia
notes: Location given as 41° or 42° S, 20° E, in close vicinity of Marzeveen/Maarseveen. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Diego Alvarez
notes: Location given as 39° 10′ S, 11° 15′ W, between Tristan da Cunha and Gough. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Dougherty Island
notes: Because it is near Antarctica, it is likely that the discoverer, Captain Dougherty, and future explorers who confirmed it, saw fog banks and icebergs conveniently situated in the right place and time.

name: Dragon Island
removed_evidence: , 136° 36′ W. Found nonexistent in 1875.
notes: Reported by Capt. Andrew of the bark Dragon at 24° 30′ N, 136° 36′ W. Found nonexistent in 1875.

name: Dunkin's Reef
removed_evidence: ive shoal. Noted as doubtful and possibly a mistaken sighting in 1851; not seen
notes: Discovered by Dunkin; location given as 9° 50′ N, 154° 10′ E. Described as an extensive shoal. Noted as doubtful and possibly a mistaken sighting in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Elizabeth Island
removed_evidence: s circumnavigation. Not found by subsequent explorers; in 1939 Felix Rie
notes: Described by Francis Drake, who reported harbouring there during his circumnavigation. Not found by subsequent explorers; in 1939 Felix Riesenberg suggested Pactolus Bank as a possible remnant, though recent surveys suggest the Bank may itself be a phantom feature.

name: Emerald Island
notes: Probably fog banks and icebergs (see Dougherty Island above); the abyssal plain below it was named Emerald Plain, however, in recognition of the nonexistent island.

name: Emily Rock
notes: Sighted at 25° 38' S, 87° 25' W by the bark Emily. Reportedly measured to be 15' tall and 120' long. 2 other sightings were reported in 1873, now described as being 3/4th mile long and 20 feet at its tallest point, made of sandy volcanic stone. Several vessels passed through the area but did not see it.

name: Ernest Legouve Reef
notes: A reef supposedly found by the captain of the French ship, Ernest Legouvé, which is near the exact location of the fictional Lincoln Island, the main setting for Jules Verne's book The Mysterious Island, also appearing in In Search of the Castaways.

name: Estotiland
notes: An island appearing on the Zeno map at the current location of Labrador.

name: Faith Island
notes: Location given as 21° 10′ S, 138° 52′ W, in the Tuamotus. Believed to be a mistaken sighting of a nearby island.

name: Fata Morgana Land
notes: J.P. Koch, together with Aage Bertelsen, was reported to have first seen Fata Morgana Land () lying in the Arctic Ocean around 80°00´N 10°00´W between NE Greenland and Svalbard. This elusive land was allegedly seen as well by Lauge Koch from the air in 1933.

name: Filippo Reef
notes: This reef, part of the Line Islands, was first seen by the ship Filippo and was seen again in 1926 when both ships saw breakers in the same area, suggesting a depth of . Current observations show the reported location to have a depth of , and the nearest shallow seamount is about deep, disproving the existence of the island.

name: Fonseca Island
notes: An island sighted east of Barbados.

name: Frisland
notes: Another island on the Zeno map, possibly a renamed Iceland.

name: Ganges Island
notes: A nonexistent island off the coast of Japan to the southwest of the Shatsky Rise.

name: Isle Grande
notes: Discovered by Antonio de la Roche. Roche only passed the island on its eastern side. Various locations given, all at 45° 15′ S, but otherwise differing at 38° 15′ W (per la Roche), 45° 30′ W, and 35° 30′ W; considered uncertain by 1808. Possibly a mistaken sighting of a projecting headland from South America, as la Roche never saw the other side.

name: Groclant
notes: An island to the west of Greenland, perhaps a misreading of the island's name, or Baffin Island.

name: Haymet Rocks
notes: Reported to be located South of Rarotonga; two rocks, about 0.25 miles apart, with 7 or 8 feet of water over them; have not been found since.

name: Humphrey Island
removed_evidence: ce and was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
notes: Discoverer unknown; location given as 16° 52' S, 140° 30' W. Krusenstern doubted its existence and was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Hyperborea
notes: Hypothetic land of a mythical people living in the far north of the known world, depicted as the mirror continent of Antarctica on the Mercator map.

name: Ilha de Vera Cruz
coord_source: Porto Seguro Brazil (Brazil mistaken for an island)
notes: A supposed 'island' found by Portuguese explorers, which turned out not to be an island but rather what is currently known as Brazil.

name: Jacquet Island
notes: An island just to the east of the Flemish Cap; it was believed to exist into the 19th century, during which cartographers discussed it as a possible midway point for the Transatlantic telegraph cable.

name: Juan de Lisboa
notes: Reported on maps as being southeast of Madagascar.

name: Jupiter Reef
notes: Nonexistent reef in the Line Islands (in fact Line Islands are more than away), to the south of the also nonexistent Ernest Legouve Reef (see above).

name: Kantia
notes: Found in 1884 by Johan Otto Polter, who, in four later expeditions through 1909, disproved the island's existence.

name: Keenan Land
coord_source: hand-approx: Beaufort Sea north of Alaska
notes: Large landmass reportedly discovered in the Arctic north of Alaska; numerous searches failed to relocate it.

name: Kentzell's Island
removed_evidence: ru in 1859. Finally disproven by a survey in 1867.
notes: Reported by Capt. Kentzell of San Francisco at approx. 40° N, 150° 30′ W. The island, 20 miles long and "very low," was said to have a large seal and sea elephant population, and therefore was kept secret by seal hunters. Searches failed to find it while sightings still came in through the 1860s, including one by the Kanrin Maru in 1859. Finally disproven by a survey in 1867.

name: Kettendyk's Droogte
notes: Location given as 33° S, 4° 25′ E, northeast of Tristan da Cunha and west of South Africa. Unsuccessfully searched for, and not seen on modern maps.

name: Kianida Island or Cianeis Insula
notes: Supposedly known in Antiquity, a large island the size of Thassos but situated off the Black Sea coast of Thrace in the present Bulgaria-Turkey border area. Depicted on the 1467 map Nona Europae Tabula by Nicolaus Germanus based on Claudius Ptolemy's Geography. According to Bulgarian geomorphologist Dinyo Kanev, probably destroyed by sea in the Middle Ages.

name: Krusenstern Rock
notes: Reported as a breaker at 22° 15' N, 175° 37' W. Capt. R. Suffern of the Craigerne reported that he was at these exact coordinates in 1897 but there was no sign of the rock.

name: L'Enfants Perdu Islands
removed_evidence: , 176° 40′ W. Found doubtful in 1875 after sea
notes: Discovered by Bougainville, variously placed at 14° 16′ S, 177° 23′ W or 14° 20′ S, 176° 40′ W. Found doubtful in 1875 after searches found no land in the area. Possibly a mistaken sighting of the Horne Islands.

name: Jane Island
removed_evidence: 10′ N, 173° 15′ W. Could not be found in 1841, and the
notes: Location given as 16° 10′ N, 173° 15′ W. Could not be found in 1841, and the island being a mistaken sighting of Johnston Atoll was ruled out due to latitude. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Los Jardines
notes: A pair of phantom islands to the east of the Marshall Islands.

name: Jesus Island
removed_evidence: and it was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
notes: Reported by Mendaña at 6° 45′ S, 171° 30′ E. Krusenstern doubted its existence and it was noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: María de Lajara or Maria Laxar
notes: Usually located northeast from Hawaii, but perhaps originally one of the Bonin Islands.

name: Maria Theresa Reef (aka Tabor Island or Tabor Reef)
notes: Another nonexistent reef in the Line Islands (in fact Line Islands are more than away), slightly to the southwest-west of the phantom island, Jupiter Reef. It is a setting for Jules Verne's book In Search of the Castaways.

name: Maria Rock
removed_evidence: off of Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.
notes: Location given as 19° 45′ N, 20° 50′ W, off of Mauritania. Could not be found in 1838.

name: Marzeveen/Maarseveen
notes: Location given as 41° or 42° S, 20° E, in close vicinity of Denia/Davia. Not seen on modern maps.

name: Maury Island
notes: Location given as 27° S, 95° 06′ W. Not seen on modern maps, but could not be located on any historical maps either.

name: Mayda or Isle of Mam
notes: A crescent-shaped island in the North Atlantic that does not appear to exist; however, there is a crescent-shaped group of seamounts deep near its described location.

name: Merrill Island
removed_evidence: ng Hawaiians. Noted doubtful in 1851; not seen
notes: Reported by Captain Harding Merrill of the Comboy at 16° 38′ S, 141° W. Reportedly inhabited by people resembling Hawaiians. Noted doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: Islas de Mesa
removed_evidence: These islands were removed from Spanish charts after James Cook landed in Hawaiʻi in 1778, and it i
notes: A Spanish navigator named Juan Gaetano charted an archipelago of islands in the Central Pacific Ocean at approximately 20° N, 138° W that he named the "Islas de Mesa," with islands named , , and . These islands were removed from Spanish charts after James Cook landed in Hawaiʻi in 1778, and it is believed that the "Islas de Mesa" are actually the Hawaiian Islands with their location recorded as being 17 degrees of longitude west of their actual location (an error of about ) due to Gaetano's inability to accurately find their longitude.

name: Minnehaha Rock
notes: Sighted by Capt. Beckwith of the Victoria at 25° 50' S, 106° 20' W. No subsequent sightings have been made.

name: Mokupāpapa
notes: Known to the Native Hawaiians as a 'flat island' (translated literally from its name) to the southwest of the island of Niʻihau, past Kaʻula, described variously as 'a five-hour sail' from the latter and 'halfway to Tahiti' and actively being traveled to in James Cook's time, but a search by the voyage's men could not find it.

name: Nachtegal Rock
notes: Seen by at 40° 20′ S, 52° 55′ E. Last seen in charts in 1878.

name: Nameless Island
removed_evidence: 70° 18′ E. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
notes: Discoverer unknown; location given as 2° 50′ S, 170° 18′ E. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: New Badalgo
notes: Location given as 18° 15′ N, 143° 40′ W. Not seen on modern maps.

name: New South Greenland
notes: Unknown odd island near Antarctica, which captain Benjamin Morrell of the ship Wasp saw while traveling north from Antarctica. He thought it to be the Antarctic Peninsula (then called New South Greenland), but his reported location during the voyage, while perfectly copying the expected path for traveling up the peninsula, was over to the east and to the north of the actual position of the Antarctic Peninsula, suggesting either a huge miscalculation in location or sightings of icebergs and fog, typical of phantom islands in the Antarctic Circle.

name: New York and Nexsen Islands
notes: Reported by a Mr. Fanning on the Betsy at 8° 9′ S, 141° 30.5′ W based on location seven hours after sighting. Smoke noted, suggesting inhabitants. Observed from four to six leagues away and not approached. Suspected in 1851 to be a mistaken sighting of two nearby islands; not seen on modern maps.

name: Nimrod Islands
notes: A group of islands between Emerald Island and Dougherty Island, both of which are nonexistent. Probably a group of icebergs together.

name: Pactolus Bank
notes: An oceanic bank deep off the west coast of Cape Horn, suggested as the remains of Elizabeth Island. A 1956 search of the area turned up no shallow areas in the reported location.

name: Passion/Paxarus Island
notes: Location given as 25° 48′ N, 136° 36′ W or 26° 12′ N, 136° W. No sign of the island could be found in 1873.

name: Mount Penglai
notes: An island thirty-thousand leagues to the east off the coast of Shandong. Associated with numerous East Asian myths and legends.

name: Pepys Island
notes: In 1683, Ambrose Cowley reported an unknown island where he thought the Falklands were, but his location was 4 degrees to the north of the Falkland Islands. While it is possible that he made a mistake in seeing a nonexistent island, it is more likely he saw one of the Falkland Islands and made a 4-degree error in his location.

name: Petermannland
notes: North of Franz Josef Land, named after August Heinrich Petermann.

name: Isle Phelipeaux
removed_evidence: A nonexistent island in Lake Superior referenced in the 1783 Treaty of
notes: A nonexistent island in Lake Superior referenced in the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

name: Podesta
notes: An island to the west of El Quisco, Chile, that was discovered to be fake in 1935 and promptly removed. Other phantom islands were also found in the vicinity in 1912 and 1858 (see Sarah Ann Island).

name: Polvaro Island
notes: Usually placed at or near 9° 20′ S, 89° E. Reportedly discovered after a Portuguese ship withdrawing from Malacca to Cape Comorin was lost nearby. Sometimes called Apaluria; sighted into the 18th century. Said to be low, woody, eight to 10 miles long. Absence noted in 1866; allegedly "exploded."

name: Recreation Island
removed_evidence: th no sign of land, removed in 1864.
notes: Location given as 15° 35′ S, 150° W, north of Tahiti. Position passed over with no sign of land, removed in 1864.

name: Reed/Redfield Rocks
notes: First sighting reported by Capt. Reed of the brig Emma at 37° 24′ N, 137° 22′ W in the Shipping Gazette. More sightings were made in varying locations in 1851, 1856, and 1866. They were said to be two rocks, 600–900 feet long and 50–40 feet across, under 3–5 fathoms of water and breakers in rough weather. Four surveys from 1871 to 1875 could not find them, but another sighting in 1889 said they were now four feet above the water. Another survey in 1902 disproved their existence, but were still marked on maps as doubtful.

name: Rivadeneyra Shoal
notes: A shoal in the eastern Pacific Ocean.

name: Ilha dos Romeiros
removed_evidence: scar and Australia. Removed from charts by 1856 or earlie
notes: Location given as 28° 40′ S, 74° E, between Madagascar and Australia. Removed from charts by 1856 or earlier.

name: Roque Piz
notes: First seen in a chart by João Teixeora, located at 6° S, 60° E. Seen on maps as late as 1865, described as being three flat islands. Likely a mistaken sighting of the Seychelles or Chagos.

name: Royal Company's Islands
removed_evidence: of Tasmania. While not found by numerous expeditions in 1840, 1889, 19
notes: A fictional island widely believed during the 19th century to be to the southwest of Tasmania. While not found by numerous expeditions in 1840, 1889, 1902, 1909, and 1912, the island was not officially removed from nautical charts until 1904.

name: Royllo
notes: A small island to the west of the mythical Antillia (see Antillia above).

name: Rupes Nigra
notes: A magnetic, black island at the exact Magnetic North Pole, invented as an explanation for why all compasses point north.

name: Saint Brendan's Island
coord_source: hand-approx: west of the Canary Islands
notes: Claimed to have been first visited in 512 by the monk St. Brendan and 14 others, along with later reports up to 1772.

name: St. Elmo
removed_evidence: umference. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen
notes: Reported by Quiros, location 21° 20' S, 143° 50' W. Said to be low, surrounded by coral reefs, with a 30 Spanish leagues circumference. Noted as doubtful in 1851; not seen on modern maps.

name: St. Matthew Island
notes: An island near the coast of Africa, roughly east-northeast of Ascension Island and possibly confused with the same latitude Annobón Island.

name: Sandy Island
removed_evidence: corded on many maps until 2012, when a s
notes: Another phantom, small island to the west of New Caledonia that was recorded on many maps until 2012, when a surveying ship passed by and disproved its existence. The current leading explanation is that the island was a raft of buoyant pumice from a recent nearby seamount eruption.

name: Sannikov Land
notes: An island near the De Long Islands, north of Russia, that probably did exist but was destroyed due to coastal erosion.

name: Sarah Ann Island
notes: A phantom island near Easter Island, similar to Podesta island. See [http://www.lib.utexas.edu/maps/onc/txu-pclmaps-oclc-8322829_r_22.jpg Operational Navigation Chart] of the United States Department of Defense.

name: Satanazes
coord_source: hand-approx: north of Antillia on the 1424 Pizzigano chart
notes: This island was originally noted on maps in 1424, originating from popular legend of devils and demons attacking ships that went into the area, but the island was subsequently removed because it obviously did not exist. The island, often drawn to the north of the mythical Antillia, was purportedly full of evil demons but was sometimes called Salvaga to avoid using the profanity "devil".

name: Saxemberg Island
notes: An odd island midway between South America and Africa that numerous captains reported seeing in 1804, 1809, and 1816. While most had conflicting reports, all of them found the island in the same location; however, none of them actually made landfall. It is possible the island was volcanic and later erupted and destroyed itself. It is also possible that they were looking at Tristan de Cunha island.

name: Schjetman Reef
notes: To the west of the Hawaiian Islands, Schjetman Reef was originally found in 1868 to be an island long and wide. Later searches in 1880, 1923, and 1924 could not find the island.

name: Sefton Reef
notes: Approx. 83°W, 37°S (southwest of Robinson Crusoe Island), noted as "position doubtful" in Operational Navigation Chart of the United States Department of Defense.

name: Terra Nova Islands
notes: Thought to lie off Oates Coast, East Antarctica.

name: Thompson Island
notes: An island in the south Atlantic Ocean discovered by the whaling ship captain George Norris; it has not been seen since 1893.

name: Thule
coord_source: hand-approx: six days' sail north of Britain (Pytheas); article coords were the modern Thule
notes: A mythical island in the far north, possibly at or above the Arctic Circle, mentioned in many works from the Roman and Medieval period. Sources in antiquity placed Thule several days travel north of Great Britain visible from Orkney; or north of Scythia. More modern scholars have suggested Thule may have been Ireland; the Estonian island of Saaremaa; or the Norwegian island of Smøla.

name: Tiburones
removed_evidence: 1° S, 143° W; noted doubtful in 1851 and not s
notes: Captain D'Urville asked the residents of Uapoa about this island in August 1838. They claimed it existed, reporting it had high land, one sandy beach which could be approached in good weather, and a single male inhabitant (the others having fled). Location given as 11° S, 143° W; noted doubtful in 1851 and not seen on modern maps.

name: Torca Island
notes: A mythical island near Ambon in Indonesia purportedly destroyed by a volcanic eruption.

name: Transit Reef
notes: A possible reef in Southern Palau. While this reef probably exists, some maps do not list it as an actual location, and, although the reef doesn't have any land, the native name of the island, Pieraurou, means 'Sandy Navigation Point', implying a sandy island or sand bar.

name: Truls Island
notes: Reported by the tanker Truls at 56° S, 23° 15′ E. Marked on USHO Chart 5188B in October 1969 as "ED" (existence doubtful).

name: Tuanaki
notes: A vanished group of islets in the Cook Islands at which a sailor allegedly spent 6 days, but a ship traveling in the waters two years later found no island.

name: Turnbull Island
removed_evidence: 43° 32′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1864 and remov
notes: Location given as 19° 52′ S, 143° 32′ W. Noted as doubtful in 1864 and removed from charts after 1875.

name: Two Brothers Reef
removed_evidence: 8° 28′ W. Existence doubtful by 1912 due to la
notes: Reportedly struck by a whaling ship in 1823, location listed as 24° 14' N, 168° 28′ W. Existence doubtful by 1912 due to lack of sightings; not seen on modern maps.

name: Wachusett Reef
notes: A nonexistent reef in the Line Islands – in fact Line Islands are more than away – along with Ernest Legouve Reef, Jupiter Reef, and Maria Theresa Reef. This reef, the largest of the three, was thought to be deep. None of these reefs are currently believed to have actually existed.

name: Walker Island
notes: A claimed "island" southeast of Hawaii reportedly discovered by a captain named Walker sometime between 1812 and 1814. It is shown slightly east of the phantom island Sarah Ann Island on some maps. Another theory suggests that it may have been confused with Washington Island.

name: Yosemite Rock
notes: Approx. 83°W, 32°S (northwest of Robinson Crusoe Island), noted as "Existence doubtful" in [http://www.lib.utexas.edu/maps/onc/txu-pclmaps-oclc-8322829_r_22.jpg Operational Navigation Chart] of the United States Department of Defense.

name: (unnamed bank)
notes: Shown on historical charts at 30° 55' N, 177° 30' E and 42 fathoms deep. Soundings of this area in 1901 and 1902 failed to locate the bottom at 100 fathoms, and it is not seen on modern maps.

name: (unnamed rock)
notes: Sighted by the steamer Great Pacific at 25° 40' S, 85° 0' W. The Sumbawa passed through the area in 1904 but did not see it.

name: (unnamed breakers)
notes: Reported at 21° 55' N, 176° 05' W. There is no indication of these breakers on modern maps.
